claims.claim: NEURON is a simulation environment that can be used to create biophysical neuron models with realistic morphologies, ionic currents, and channel densities.
claims.source: Simulation environments like NEURON (Hines and Carnevale, 2001; Carnevale and Hines, 2006) can be used to create biophysical neuron models with realistic morphologies, ionic currents, and channel densities (Figure 1A), facilitating the integration of experimental data into models (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995; Stuart and Spruston, 1998; Migliore et al., 1999; Poirazi et al., 2003; Destexhe and Paré, 1999; Traub et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the NEURON documentation and examples of its use, as well as Figure 1A showing the components of biophysical neuron models.

claims.claim: More than a thousand neuronal models are archived in ModelDB.
claims.source: More than a thousand neuronal models, and several thousand individual ion channel models, are archived in the online database ModelDB (Hines et al., 2004), which enables other researchers to verify original claims, and to reuse and extend existing neuron models in the light of new results.
claims.evidence: This is a factual claim about the ModelDB database, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Several thousand individual ion channel models are archived in ModelDB.
claims.source: More than a thousand neuronal models, and several thousand individual ion channel models, are archived in the online database ModelDB (Hines et al., 2004), which enables other researchers to verify original claims, and to reuse and extend existing neuron models in the light of new results.
claims.evidence: This is a factual claim about the ModelDB database, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Replacing the A-type potassium channel model in a layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron model with different A-type models from ModelDB changes the neuron's dynamics.
claims.source: However, the dynamics can change, sometimes dramatically, when one of the modeled ion channel currents is exchanged for an identically-labeled model from a different publication on ModelDB (Figure 1B, colored traces, Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 1B and 1C, where different ion channel models produce different neuronal behaviors.

claims.claim: Over 300 new ion channel models were added to ModelDB in 2014 alone.
claims.source: Furthermore, the increasingly large number of models on ModelDB (e.g., over 300 new ion channel models in 2014 alone; Shepherd Lab [2015]), with non-standardized labeling and a high degree of redundancy, makes it difficult to understand how ion channel models relate to each other and to biology.
claims.evidence: This is a factual claim about ModelDB growth, supported by citation to Shepherd Lab 2015.

claims.claim: There are over 250 A-type potassium channel models on ModelDB.
claims.source: For example, a researcher looking to use an existing A-type potassium channel model will find over 250 A-type models, spanning a range of behaviors (Figure 1C, blue).
claims.evidence: This is a factual claim about the number of A-type models in ModelDB, demonstrated in the analysis and shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: A-type potassium channel models on ModelDB span a range of behaviors.
claims.source: For example, a researcher looking to use an existing A-type potassium channel model will find over 250 A-type models, spanning a range of behaviors (Figure 1C, blue).
claims.evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 1C, where different A-type models produce different outcomes.

claims.claim: It is common for modelers to adapt previously published ion channel models for their own purposes.
claims.source: Instead of a thorough and time-consuming fitting of appropriate ion channel dynamics, it is common for modelers to adapt previously published ion channel models for their own purposes.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about modeling practice, supported by the genealogy analysis showing ancestor-descendant relationships among models.

claims.claim: Adapting previously published ion channel models may introduce experimentally unverified systematic changes or errors into later generations of models.
claims.source: However, this may introduce experimentally unverified systematic changes or even errors into later generations of models and may have dramatic effects on the biological interpretation of the results.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential consequences of model reuse, based on logical inference.

claims.claim: The study cataloged all relevant information about each ion channel model from the associated literature, including pedigree relations.
claims.source: We cataloged all relevant information about each ion channel model from the associated literature, including its pedigree relations: whether a given ion channel model is based on previous models, and, if so, which ones.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological approach taken in the study.

claims.claim: The study compared the kinetics of each ion channel model in standardized voltage-clamp protocols.
claims.source: Additionally, we compared the kinetics of each ion channel model in standardized voltage-clamp protocols.
claims.evidence: This describes a key methodological approach of the study, detailed in the Methods section.

claims.claim: The study grouped 2378 ion channel models into 211 clusters.
claims.source: Our efforts have grouped 2378 ion channel models into 211 clusters, dramatically simplifying the search for an appropriate ion channel model.
claims.evidence: This is a primary result of the study, supported by the clustering analysis.

claims.claim: The underlying database is freely and programmatically accessible via a web API.
claims.source: The underlying database is freely and programmatically accessible via a web application programming interface (API).
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of the resource created by the study.

claims.claim: The resource allows uploading and assessment of experimentally recorded current traces.
claims.source: In an effort to make our resource compatible with experimental data and new ion channel models, we offer the possibility to upload and assess the similarity of experimentally recorded current traces (as well as new models and model traces) in the same topology.
claims.evidence: This describes a capability of the resource, demonstrated in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The study analyzed an unclassified ion channel model as an example of using the comparison framework.
claims.source: We show an example of the use of this comparison through the analysis of an unclassified ion channel model, as well as an experimentally recorded voltage-dependent potassium current from Drosophila melanogaster.
claims.evidence: This describes an example application shown in the results, specifically in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The study analyzed an experimentally recorded voltage-dependent potassium current from Drosophila melanogaster.
claims.source: We show an example of the use of this comparison through the analysis of an unclassified ion channel model, as well as an experimentally recorded voltage-dependent potassium current from Drosophila melanogaster.
claims.evidence: This describes an example application shown in the results, specifically in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The study categorized 2378 voltage- and calcium-dependent ion channel models in NEURON available on ModelDB.
claims.source: To build a map of ion channel model function, we categorized and analyzed a widely-used subset of 2378 voltage- and calcium-dependent ion channel models ('.mod' files) in the NEURON simulation environment (Hines and Carnevale, 2001; Carnevale and Hines, 2006).
claims.evidence: This describes the scope of the analysis performed in the study.

claims.claim: Metadata was extracted manually from associated journal articles for each ion channel model file.
claims.source: A set of 'metadata' was extracted manually from the associated journal articles for each ion channel model file (Figure 2A, top): reference information (Ref. Info, including author(s) of the model code), ion channel information (I.C. Info: ion selectivity, gating mode, subtype), system information (Sys. Info: brain area, neuron type, neuron region, animal model), as well as additional comments (Other: e.g. temperature constraints, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for metadata collection, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The majority of all ion channel models (~75%) fell into five classes based on ion selectivity and gating mode.
claims.source: Based on ion selectivity and gating mode, the majority of all ion channel models (~75%) fell into five classes (Figure 2B): voltage-dependent potassium (Kv), voltage-dependent sodium (Nav), voltage- dependent calcium (Cav), calcium-dependent potassium (KCa) and hyperpolarization-activated cation (Ih) channel models.
claims.evidence: This is a result of the classification analysis, shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: 74 different subtype labels were recorded across all five ion channel classes.
claims.source: We recorded 74 different subtype labels across all classes (Kv: 32, Nav: 19, Cav: 20, KCa: 11, Ih: 5; Figure 2B, cf. Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the metadata analysis.

claims.claim: Prominent modeled neuron types were pyramidal, interneuron, granule cell, and basket cell.
claims.source: Prominent modeled neuron types were pyramidal, interneuron, granule cell, and basket cell (Figure 2C), and prominent brain areas included hippocampus, and cortex (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the metadata analysis, shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Prominent brain areas modeled included hippocampus and cortex.
claims.source: Prominent modeled neuron types were pyramidal, interneuron, granule cell, and basket cell (Figure 2C), and prominent brain areas included hippocampus, and cortex (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the metadata analysis, shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Many ion channel models form large families with a highly-cited hub model that has many descendants.
claims.source: Visualizing family relationships makes it apparent that many ion channel models form large families, often with a highly-cited hub model that has many descendants (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the genealogy analysis, illustrated in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: There are a large number of small families and model singletons that imply de novo ion channel model creation, lack of appropriate citations, or translation from other simulators.
claims.source: On the other hand, there are a large number of small families and model singletons that imply de novo ion channel model creation, lack of appropriate citations, or translation from other simulators (noted in the metadatum comments).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the genealogy analysis results, with possible explanations inferred from the data.

claims.claim: Subtype labeling mapped well onto families, but family identity did not guarantee homogeneity of subtype or vice versa.
claims.source: Subtype labeling mapped well onto families, but family identity did not guarantee homogeneity of subtype or vice versa – all individual subtypes were found across several families (see Figure 2E for Kv, and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2A,F for other ion type classes).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing subtype labels with family relationships, shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Five voltage-clamp simulation protocols were used to quantify functional relationships between ion channel models.
claims.source: To quantify the functional relationships between ion channel models, we used a set of voltage-clamp simulation protocols, in kind with those developed for the experimental characterization of ion channels and model fitting (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952b; Willms et al., 1999; Ranjan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, with citations to related work.

claims.claim: The voltage-clamp protocols were designed to probe activation, deactivation, inactivation, temporal dynamics during voltage ramping, and repeated action potentials.
claims.source: The protocols were designed to probe the gating characteristics of ion channels, that is, activation, deactivation and inactivation, as well as temporal dynamics during voltage ramping and repeated action potentials.
claims.evidence: This describes the design rationale for the voltage-clamp protocols used in the study.

claims.claim: Principal component analysis was used to obtain a D-dimensional score for each ion channel model, accounting for at least 99% of variance.
claims.source: Using principal component analysis (PCA) across all traces of a particular ion channel type, we obtained a final D-dimensional score for each ion channel model, accounting for at least 99% of the variance across all channel models in each class.
claims.evidence: This describes the dimensionality reduction methodology used in the analysis.

claims.claim: The dimensionality D varied between 16 and 29 dimensions for the five ion channel classes.
claims.source: The dimensionality D varied between 16 and 29 dimensions for the five classes (Kv: 16, Nav: 21, Cav: 29, KCa: 16, Ih: 16).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the PCA analysis.

claims.claim: Ward's clustering method was used to establish an agglomerative hierarchy of ion channel model clusters.
claims.source: Finally, we used Ward's clustering method (Ward, 1963) on the model scores to establish an agglomerative hierarchy of ion channel model clusters (Figure 3C, bottom).
claims.evidence: This describes the clustering methodology, with citation to Ward 1963.

claims.claim: The Kv class was divided into 60 clusters with distinct responses.
claims.source: For the Kv class, this resulted in 60 clusters with distinct responses (Figure 4) and small intra-cluster variability (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is a result of the clustering analysis for the Kv class.

claims.claim: The Nav, Cav, KCa, and Ih classes divided into 38, 43, 44, and 26 clusters respectively.
claims.source: The other classes divided similarly into 38, 43, 44, and 26 clusters for Nav, Cav, KCa, and Ih, respectively (see Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result of the clustering analysis for the other ion channel classes.

claims.claim: Most ancestor-descendant families fell within one cluster, indicating consistency between family relations and ion channel model behavior.
claims.source: We found that most ancestor-descendant families fell within one cluster, indicating consistency between the family relations collected from the papers and ion channel model behavior (Figure 4A–B, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2B,C and G,H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparing genealogy with clustering results, shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: A common subtype label did not guarantee a common cluster identity.
claims.source: However, a common subtype label did not guarantee a common cluster identity (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2C,H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparing subtype labels with clustering results.

claims.claim: The ~250 A-type-labeled Kv ion channel models fell into 14 clusters.
claims.source: For example, the ~250 A-type-labeled Kv ion channel models fell into 14 clusters (although only five clusters comprised over 90% of them, Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a specific result from the clustering analysis of A-type Kv models.

claims.claim: Five A-type Kv clusters comprised over 90% of A-type models.
claims.source: For example, the ~250 A-type-labeled Kv ion channel models fell into 14 clusters (although only five clusters comprised over 90% of them, Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the clustering analysis.

claims.claim: For four of the five ion type classes (KCa being the exception), most isolated single-model clusters corresponded to genealogical singletons.
claims.source: Interestingly, for four of the five ion type classes (KCa being the exception), most isolated single-model clusters corresponded to genealogical singletons, supporting the idea that these ion channel models are indeed unique, and do not appear isolated simply due to missing ancestor-descendant links.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing clustering results with genealogy data.

claims.claim: Individual neurons of any given type display heterogeneity in ion channel expression and regulation.
claims.source: There is substantial evidence that individual neurons of any given type display heterogeneity in ion channel expression and regulation (Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Schulz et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Characterizing an ionic current using the average response across a population may not be sufficient to capture appropriate behavior at the neuronal level.
claims.source: Furthermore, characterizing an ionic current using the average response across a population may not be sufficient to capture the appropriate behavior at the neuronal level (Golowasch et al., 2002), as there may be several distinct 'solutions' (Prinz et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Diversity and variation in ionic currents within a single cell type may arise from mechanisms such as splice variants, differential subunit combination, and post-translational modification.
claims.source: Diversity and variation in ionic currents even within a single cell type may arise from such mechanisms as splice variants, differential subunit combination, and post-translational modification like phosphorylation (Schulz et al., 2008; Li et al., 2007; Campiglio and Flucher, 2015; Levitan, 1994; Misonou et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The behavior of groups of ion channel models defined by common subtype, neuron type and brain area is often more diverse than that of models defined by a common cluster.
claims.source: Consistent with this notion, the behavior of groups of ion channel models defined by common subtype, neuron type and brain area (Figure 5A, plotted data points) is often more diverse than that of models defined by a common cluster (Figure 5A, dashed line).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the analysis comparing metadata-based groupings with cluster-based groupings, shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: There is no clear correspondence of any given cluster with categories such as brain area and neuron type.
claims.source: More specifically, we find no clear correspondence of any given cluster with categories such as brain area and neuron type (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the analysis, illustrated in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Nearly every cluster contains ion channel models that have been used in pyramidal cells of both cortex and hippocampus.
claims.source: Nearly every cluster contains ion channel models that have been used in pyramidal cells (Figure 5B, left, blue) of both cortex and hippocampus (Figure 5B, right, blue and green).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: A-type-labeled models used in pyramidal cells of the hippocampus (117 models) are found in nine clusters.
claims.source: In the same vein, e.g., A-type-labeled models that have been used in pyramidal cells of the hippocampus (117 models) are found in nine clusters (cf. ICGenealogy, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from the analysis.

claims.claim: The analysis framework enables automated analysis of new ion channel models.
claims.source: Our analysis framework, accessible through the web interface, enables the automated analysis of new ion channel models as well as experimental data (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This describes a capability of the resource, illustrated in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The analysis framework enables automated analysis of experimental data.
claims.source: Our analysis framework, accessible through the web interface, enables the automated analysis of new ion channel models as well as experimental data (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This describes a capability of the resource, illustrated in Figure 6A and demonstrated in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: An uncatalogued Kv model from a hippocampus CA1 pyramidal cell model (kad.mod from Hsu et al. 2015) fits well within a cluster of mostly pyramidal A-type-labeled ion channel models used in simulations of rodent hippocampus.
claims.source: We found that the ion channel model fits well within a cluster of mostly pyramidal A-type-labeled ion channel models used in simulations of rodent hippocampus, thereby verifying the assumed characteristics of the model.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the example analysis of a new model, shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Voltage-gated cationic currents across the membranes of Drosophila Kenyon cells are thought to be dominated by A-type K+ channels, in particular Shal/Kv4.
claims.source: Voltage-gated cationic currents across the membranes of these neurons are thought to be dominated by A-type K+ channels, in particular Shal/Kv4 (Gasque et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gasque et al. 2005.

claims.claim: Experimental recordings from Drosophila Kenyon cells revealed a close match to a mammalian Kv4 ion channel model (Kv4_csi, ModelDB ID no. 145672).
claims.source: The comparison revealed a close match to an existing model from our resource, and thus characterizes the behavior of the ion channel as similar to a mammalian Kv4 ion channel (Figure 6C; Fineberg et al. (2012); Kv4_csi, ModelDB ID no. 145672).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the experimental data comparison, shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The study performed a meta-analysis of voltage- and calcium-dependent ion channel models coded in NEURON available in ModelDB.
claims.source: Here, we have performed a meta-analysis of voltage- and calcium-dependent ion channel models coded in the NEURON programming language available in the database ModelDB (Hines et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This describes the scope and nature of the study.

claims.claim: The approach of combining metadata with kinetics-based analysis allowed detailed information regarding the identity of each ion channel model.
claims.source: Our approach of combining metadata extracted from publications with a kinetics-based analysis allowed us to provide detailed information regarding the identity of each ion channel model in the resource, filling in missing or ambiguous data, and validating the functional properties of channel models against their sometimes ambiguous nomenclature.
claims.evidence: This describes the contribution of the study's methodology.

claims.claim: The framework provides a unified characterization of ion channel function for large-scale comparison of models with each other and with experiments.
claims.source: Furthermore, we provide a framework for the large-scale comparison of models, both with each other and with experiments using the same standardized protocols, thus paving the way towards a unified characterization of ion channel function.
claims.evidence: This describes the contribution and potential impact of the study.

claims.claim: The voltage-clamp protocols used were designed to efficiently probe the kinetics of all ion channel types considered.
claims.source: The voltage-clamp protocols used in this study were designed to efficiently probe the kinetics of all ion channel types considered here (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952b; Willms et al., 1999; Ranjan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes the design rationale for the protocols, with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Measuring kinetic responses allowed comparison of models regardless of their specific implementation.
claims.source: Measuring the kinetic responses of each channel model allowed us to compare models regardless of their specific implementation.
claims.evidence: This describes an advantage of the methodology used.

claims.claim: The simplicity of the protocols makes experimental comparison easier.
claims.source: Additionally, the simplicity of our protocols makes experimental comparison easier.

claims.claim: The same protocols can be used to integrate models written for other simulators or simulator-independent formats like NeuroML.

claims.evidence: This describes potential extensions of the approach, with citation to NeuroML.

claims.claim: Of the 2378 models in the resource, 1132 models were identified as unique.
claims.source: Of the 2378 models in our resource, we could identify 1132 models as unique, and further reduced this to 211 groups with substantially different kinetics.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claims.claim: The 1132 unique models were further reduced to 211 groups with substantially different kinetics.
claims.source: Of the 2378 models in our resource, we could identify 1132 models as unique, and further reduced this to 211 groups with substantially different kinetics.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claims.claim: The partition of channel models into clusters does not imply that models in the same cluster are necessarily redundant.
claims.source: However, this does not eliminate the task of finding the most appropriate ion channel model current, and we stress that the partition of channel models into clusters of similar response properties does not imply that models in the same cluster are necessarily redundant.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary statement about interpreting the clustering results.

claims.claim: Intra-cluster differences may still be important depending on the particular simulation at hand.
claims.source: Intra-cluster differences may still be important depending on the particular simulation at hand.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the practical use of the clustering results.

claims.claim: The responses of different channels vary slowly and continuously rather than in discrete steps along the dimensions of the manifold of scores.
claims.source: Since the responses of different channels vary slowly and continuously rather than in discrete steps along the dimensions of the manifold of scores (see e.g. Figure 4B), the data may also be amenable to more sophisticated clustering and machine-learning approaches.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the structure of the data, with reference to Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The raw response data and scores have been made publicly available.
claims.source: To this end, the raw response data and scores have been made publicly available (ICGenealogy, 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes a data availability feature of the resource.

claims.claim: The variability in behavior of ionic currents suggests there is no clear answer to which ion channel model to use for a given neuronal simulation.
claims.source: Furthermore, the variability in behavior of ionic currents seen here and elsewhere (Marder and Goaillard, 2006) suggests that there is no clear answer to the question of which ion channel model (and parameters) to use for a given neuronal simulation at hand.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, with supporting citation.

claims.claim: Neuron model parameters should be viewed as regions rather than as individual representative points in parameter space.
claims.source: On a larger scope, it has been suggested previously that neuron model parameters should be viewed as regions, rather than as individual representative points in parameter space (Goldman et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Goldman et al. 2001.

claims.claim: The variability at the level of individual ion channel models may cover regions in parameter space and organize into distinct 'solutions' to particular model behaviors.
claims.source: It may be possible that the variability seen at the level of individual ion channel models covers such regions, and organizes into a handful of distinct 'solutions' to particular model behaviors on the neuronal scale (O'Leary et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the interpretation of variability, with supporting citation.

claims.claim: The database could be used for systematic analyses of co-variability of sets of published ion channel models that elicit desired behaviors in conductance-based neuron models.
claims.source: In this sense, our database would lend itself to systematic analyses of the co-variability of sets of published ion channel models that are able to elicit desired behaviors in conductance-based neuron models (see also Figure 1), in line with previous work (Prinz et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This describes a potential application of the resource, with supporting citation.

claims.claim: The interactive browser acts as a complement to existing resources such as ModelDB.
claims.source: We provide an interactive browser (ICGenealogy, 2016), which acts as a complement to existing resources such as ModelDB.
claims.evidence: This describes the relationship of the resource to existing databases.

claims.claim: The voltage-clamp protocols are inspired by experimental procedures, allowing direct comparison of ion channel models to experiments.
claims.source: Because our voltage-clamp protocols are inspired by experimental procedures, ion channel models can be compared directly to experiments in an automated fashion.
claims.evidence: This describes an advantage of the protocol design for experimental comparison.

claims.claim: The resource will enable better experimentally-constrained modeling.
claims.source: Beyond its usefulness for cataloguing ion channel model behavior and pedigree, our resource will enable better experimentally-constrained modeling, and presents a first step towards a unified functional map of ion channel dynamics in model and experiment.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the expected impact of the resource.

claims.claim: The resource presents a first step towards a unified functional map of ion channel dynamics in model and experiment.
claims.source: Beyond its usefulness for cataloguing ion channel model behavior and pedigree, our resource will enable better experimentally-constrained modeling, and presents a first step towards a unified functional map of ion channel dynamics in model and experiment.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the contribution and future direction of the work.

claims.claim: A layer 2/3 pyramidal cell model was adapted from Traub et al. (2003), ModelDB ID no. 20756.
claims.source: A model of a layer 2/3 pyramidal cell was adapted from a previous study (Traub et al., 2003), ModelDB ID no. 20756.
claims.evidence: This describes the source of the neuron model used in Figure 1.

claims.source: The total number of files collected from the database was 3495.

claims.claim: The five ion channel groups (Kv, Nav, Cav, KCa, Ih) accounted for 2378 files.
claims.source: These five groups accounted for 2378 files, references for which are available in Supplementary file 2.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the classification process.

claims.source: A substantial number of .mod files (952 files) had to be slightly modified to work with the procedure, in one of the following ways: (1) reversal potential was renamed and made a global variable to be accessed from .hoc file, (2) NONSPECIFIC CURRENT was changed to a USEION statement with the correct ion type (3) extra functions and/or data were included through .inc files, data tables or extra .mod files (4) max conductance was made nonzero (arbitrarily set to 1.0) (5) file was split into multiple files for each current present (6) POINTER variables were removed (7) internal temperature initialization was removed, and temperature dependence was set to use the global variable 'celsius'.

claims.source: The most recent version at the time of writing, version 7.3, of the NEURON language (Carnevale and Hines, 2014) was used to run the simulation protocols.
claims.evidence: This describes the software version used in the analysis.

claims.source: All simulations were run in Ubuntu 12.04.5 on a single core of a Intel Core i7 @ 2.67 GHz with 24 Gigabytes of RAM.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational environment used for simulations.

claims.claim: The maximum current amplitude depends on the number of channel models in a particular area and is not related to the kinetic behavior of the channels.
claims.source: We reasoned that the maximum current amplitude depends on the number of channel models in a particular area and was thus not related to the kinetic behavior of the channels.
claims.evidence: This is a rationale for the normalization procedure.

claims.claim: Ward's minimal variance linkage for hierarchical clustering was used as implemented in the MATLAB Statistics Toolbox.
claims.source: For clustering of channel scores, we used Ward's minimal variance linkage (Ward, 1963) for hierarchical clustering, as implemented in the MATLAB Statistics Toolbox (R2015A, The MathWorks Inc., Natick, MA).
claims.evidence: This describes the clustering method and software used.

claims.claim: Several cluster indexes were employed to determine an appropriate number of clusters: Silhouette criterion, Dunn index, Davies-Bouldin index, and Calinski-Harabasz measure.
claims.source: To this end we employed a range of internal clustering evaluation measures, which indicate the emergence of an appropriate number of clusters. Although the evaluation of these measures requires some heuristics, they have been well established and can guide the decision as to which number of clusters to choose. Concretely, these are: the Silhouette criterion (Rousseeuw, 1987), the Dunn index (Dunn, 1973), the Davies-Bouldin index (Davies and Bouldin, 1979), and the Calinski-Harabasz measure (Calinski and Harabasz, 1974), also implemented in the MATLAB Statistics Toolbox (R2015A, The MathWorks Inc., Natick, MA).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for determining cluster numbers, with citations to the methods.

claims.claim: K+ currents were recorded from Drosophila Kenyon cells in targeted in vivo whole-cell voltage clamp experiments.
claims.source: K+ currents were recorded from Drosophila Kenyon cells in targeted in vivo whole-cell voltage clamp experiments as previously described (Murthy and Turner, 2013).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology, with citation.

claims.claim: Male NP7175-GAL4;UAS-mCD8-GFP flies were used for electrophysiology experiments.
claims.source: Male NP7175-GAL4;UAS-mCD8-GFP flies were immobilized and fixed to a perfusion chamber using wax.

results.result: The study analyzed 2378 voltage- and calcium-dependent ion channel models from ModelDB coded in NEURON, classified them into five major ion channel classes (Kv, Nav, Cav, KCa, Ih) representing ~75% of models, identified 1132 unique models, and grouped them into 211 clusters with substantially different kinetics (Kv: 60, Nav: 38, Cav: 43, KCa: 44, Ih: 26 clusters).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C21, C26, C28, C40, C41, C68, and C69 collectively describe the main quantitative results of the clustering analysis. The numbers are consistent across claims and are supported by the methodology described (voltage-clamp protocols, PCA, Ward's clustering). The classification into five ion channel classes and the specific cluster numbers for each class are clearly stated and form the core contribution of the work.

results.result: Metadata was manually extracted from journal articles for each ion channel model, including 74 different subtype labels across all classes, with prominent modeled neuron types being pyramidal, interneuron, granule cell, and basket cell, and prominent brain areas being hippocampus and cortex. Pedigree relations (ancestor-descendant relationships) were also cataloged.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C29, C30, C31, and C19 describe the metadata collection methodology and results. The manual extraction process is clearly described, and the quantitative results (74 subtypes, prominent cell types and brain areas) are presented in Figure 2. The genealogy analysis is a key methodological component that is well-documented.

results.result: Five voltage-clamp simulation protocols were designed to probe activation, deactivation, inactivation, temporal dynamics during voltage ramping, and repeated action potentials. Principal component analysis was used to obtain a D-dimensional score for each ion channel model (accounting for at least 99% of variance), with dimensionality varying between 16 and 29 dimensions across the five ion channel classes.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C36, C37, C38, and C62 describe the core methodology for functional characterization. The voltage-clamp protocols are well-documented in the methods section and supplementary materials (Figure 3, Tables 1-2), and the PCA approach with 99% variance criterion is clearly specified. The dimensionality values for each class are explicitly stated.

results.result: Ward's clustering method was used to establish an agglomerative hierarchy of ion channel model clusters, with the number of clusters determined using multiple cluster indexes (Silhouette criterion, Dunn index, Davies-Bouldin index, and Calinski-Harabasz measure).
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C94, and C95 describe the clustering methodology. Ward's method is a well-established approach, properly cited, and the use of multiple cluster validation indexes is appropriate and well-documented in Figure 3 supplements 2-3. The methodology is sound and reproducible.

results.result: Many ion channel models form large families with highly-cited hub models that have many descendants, while there are also many small families and singletons. Subtype labeling mapped well onto families, but family identity did not guarantee homogeneity of subtype or vice versa. Most ancestor-descendant families fell within one cluster, indicating consistency between family relations and ion channel model behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C33, C34, and C42 describe findings from the genealogy analysis. These observations are supported by Figure 2E and Figure 4A-B, which visualize family relationships and their correspondence with clusters. The finding that most families fall within single clusters validates the consistency between genealogical and functional relationships.

results.result: A common subtype label did not guarantee a common cluster identity. The ~250 A-type-labeled Kv ion channel models fell into 14 clusters (with five clusters comprising over 90% of them), and A-type-labeled models used in pyramidal cells of the hippocampus (117 models) are found in nine clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, C45, and C53 describe the heterogeneity within subtype labels, using A-type Kv channels as a specific example. This is well-documented in Figure 4B and demonstrates that traditional nomenclature does not capture functional diversity. The quantitative results are specific and supported by the data.

results.result: The behavior of groups of ion channel models defined by common subtype, neuron type and brain area is often more diverse than that of models defined by a common cluster. There is no clear correspondence of any given cluster with categories such as brain area and neuron type, with nearly every cluster containing ion channel models used in pyramidal cells of both cortex and hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C51, and C52 describe the relationship between metadata-based groupings and functional clusters, supported by Figure 5A-B. The finding that functional similarity does not correspond to traditional biological categories is important for understanding ion channel diversity and is well-demonstrated by the data.

results.result: The IonChannelGenealogy (ICGenealogy) web interface provides an interactive resource for categorization of ion channel models and experimental recordings, with the underlying database freely and programmatically accessible via a web API. The analysis framework enables automated analysis of new ion channel models and experimental data, and acts as a complement to existing resources such as ModelDB.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C22, C54, C55, and C78 describe the web resource and its capabilities. The resource is demonstrated throughout the manuscript (Figure 7) and its functionality for analyzing new models and experimental data is shown in Figure 6. This represents a significant practical contribution of the work.

results.result: An uncatalogued Kv model from a hippocampus CA1 pyramidal cell model (kad.mod from Hsu et al. 2015) was analyzed and found to fit well within a cluster of mostly pyramidal A-type-labeled ion channel models used in simulations of rodent hippocampus, thereby verifying the assumed characteristics of the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C56 and C24 describe a validation example showing that the framework can correctly classify a new model. This is demonstrated in Figure 6B and provides evidence that the clustering captures meaningful functional relationships. The result validates the utility of the resource.

results.result: Experimental recordings from Drosophila Kenyon cells (known to be dominated by A-type K+ channels, particularly Shal/Kv4) revealed a close match to a mammalian Kv4 ion channel model (Kv4_csi, ModelDB ID no. 145672) when analyzed using the framework.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C25, C57, C96, and C97 describe the experimental validation using Drosophila recordings. The experimental methodology is properly described and cited (Murthy and Turner, 2013), and the results shown in Figure 6C demonstrate that the framework can match experimental data to appropriate models. This validates the biological relevance of the approach.

results.result: Replacing the A-type potassium channel model in a layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron model with different A-type models from ModelDB changes the neuron's dynamics, sometimes dramatically. There are over 250 A-type potassium channel models on ModelDB spanning a range of behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C15, and C16 describe the motivating observation that identically-labeled models can produce different neuronal behaviors. This is demonstrated in Figure 1B-C using simulations of a pyramidal neuron model with different ion channel models. The result effectively motivates the need for the study.

results.result: Individual neurons of any given type display heterogeneity in ion channel expression and regulation. Characterizing an ionic current using the average response across a population may not be sufficient to capture appropriate behavior at the neuronal level. Diversity and variation in ionic currents within a single cell type may arise from mechanisms such as splice variants, differential subunit combination, and post-translational modification.
results.evaluation: Claims C47, C48, and C49 describe biological context from the literature, supported by multiple citations (Marder and Goaillard 2006, Schulz et al. 2008, Golowasch et al. 2002, Prinz et al. 2004, Li et al. 2007, Campiglio and Flucher 2015, Levitan 1994, Misonou et al. 2004). These claims provide important biological context for interpreting the observed variability in ion channel models.

results.result: The approach of combining metadata with kinetics-based analysis allowed detailed information regarding the identity of each ion channel model, filling in missing or ambiguous data and validating functional properties against nomenclature. The framework provides a unified characterization of ion channel function for large-scale comparison of models with each other and with experiments, enabling better experimentally-constrained modeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C61, C79, C80, and C81 describe the overall contribution and impact of the work. These claims are supported by the demonstrated capabilities of the resource (metadata collection, functional clustering, experimental comparison) and represent reasonable conclusions about the utility of the framework.

results.result: A total of 3495 .mod files were collected from ModelDB, of which 366 were tools or other non-ion channel items, and the five ion channel groups (Kv, Nav, Cav, KCa, Ih) accounted for 2378 files. A substantial number of files (952) had to be slightly modified to work with the procedure, and 44 files were omitted due to problems with running the simulation protocols.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C85, C86, C87, and C88 describe the data collection and preprocessing steps. These are straightforward methodological details that are clearly documented. The modifications made to files are explicitly listed, and the number of excluded files is small relative to the total dataset.

results.result: The partition of channel models into clusters does not imply that models in the same cluster are necessarily redundant, and intra-cluster differences may still be important depending on the particular simulation. The responses of different channels vary slowly and continuously rather than in discrete steps along the dimensions of the manifold of scores. The raw response data and scores have been made publicly available.
results.evaluation: Claims C70, C71, C72, and C73 provide important caveats about interpreting the clustering results and describe data availability. These are appropriate cautionary statements that acknowledge the limitations of the clustering approach while noting that the data structure is continuous. The public data availability is a strength.

results.result: The variability in behavior of ionic currents suggests there is no clear answer to which ion channel model to use for a given neuronal simulation. Neuron model parameters should be viewed as regions rather than as individual representative points in parameter space. The variability at the level of individual ion channel models may cover regions in parameter space and organize into distinct 'solutions' to particular model behaviors. The database could be used for systematic analyses of co-variability of sets of published ion channel models.
results.evaluation: Claims C74, C75, C76, and C77 present interpretations and speculations about the implications of the observed variability. While C74 and C75 are supported by citations, C76 is explicitly speculative ('It may be possible that...'), and C77 describes a potential future application. These claims go beyond what is directly demonstrated in the current study.

results.result: Ion channel models are the building blocks of computational neuron models, and their biological fidelity is crucial for the interpretation of simulations. However, the number of published models and lack of standardization make comparison difficult.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C3 establish the foundational motivation for the study. These are well-established principles in computational neuroscience (C1, C2) and the difficulty of comparison (C3) is demonstrated by the analysis of ModelDB and the example in Figure 1.

results.result: Ion channels play crucial roles in neuronal signal processing and plasticity. Interactions among different ion channels can lead to complex dynamics requiring computational modeling, as first demonstrated by Hodgkin and Huxley for action potential generation. NEURON is a simulation environment for creating biophysical neuron models, and ModelDB archives more than a thousand neuronal models and several thousand ion channel models.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C12 provide background context about ion channels, computational modeling, and existing resources. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to the literature and represent established knowledge in the field. These provide necessary context for the study.

results.result: It is common for modelers to adapt previously published ion channel models for their own purposes. However, this may introduce experimentally unverified systematic changes or errors into later generations of models and may have dramatic effects on the biological interpretation of results.
results.evaluation: Claims C17 and C18 describe modeling practices and potential consequences. C17 is supported by the genealogy analysis showing extensive model reuse (Figure 2E), while C18 is a logical inference about potential risks of model reuse. Together they motivate the need for systematic cataloging and comparison.

results.result: Measuring kinetic responses allowed comparison of models regardless of their specific implementation. Simple step and ramp current pulses are sufficient to probe underlying kinetics of neurons, and the simplicity of the protocols makes experimental comparison easier. The study was limited to voltage-dependent and calcium-dependent ion channel models coded in NEURON, but the same protocols can be used to integrate models written for other simulators or simulator-independent formats like NeuroML.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 describe advantages and limitations of the methodology. The advantages (C63, C65) are logical consequences of the approach, C64 is supported by citation to Druckmann et al. 2011, and the limitations and potential extensions (C66, C67) are appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: For four of the five ion type classes (KCa being the exception), most isolated single-model clusters corresponded to genealogical singletons, supporting the idea that these ion channel models are indeed unique and do not appear isolated simply due to missing ancestor-descendant links.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 describes a finding that validates the genealogy analysis by showing that functionally isolated models are also genealogically isolated (except for KCa). This provides evidence that the genealogy collection was reasonably complete and that functional uniqueness corresponds to genealogical uniqueness.

results.result: A layer 2/3 pyramidal cell model was adapted from Traub et al. (2003), ModelDB ID no. 20756. Version 7.3 of the NEURON language was used to run simulation protocols on Ubuntu 12.04.5 on a single core of an Intel Core i7 @ 2.67 GHz with 24 Gigabytes of RAM. The maximum current amplitude was reasoned to depend on the number of channel models in a particular area and was thus not related to the kinetic behavior of the channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C89, C90, and C93 provide methodological details about the neuron model used for demonstration (C82), computational environment (C89, C90), and rationale for normalization (C93). These are straightforward methodological details that are adequately documented.
